task: Write one sentence of your own using the word winsome. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know winsome should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bakery's winsome new apprentice — all freckles, cowlicks, and eager questions — has doubled the number of regulars who stay to chat.
Pleasant is agreeable, easy company — milder than winsome, which actively draws you in.
Irresistible goes further than winsome — a winsome smile invites you to smile back; an irresistible one has already decided the matter for you.

Charming is the broad umbrella word for pleasing, attractive ways — a diplomat, a salesman, and a toddler can all be charming. Winsome is one sweet corner of that umbrella: charm that is innocent, unstudied, and usually young. Every winsome person is charming; most charming people are not winsome.

Endearing means inspiring fondness — a lovable flaw, a snore, or a stubborn old habit can be endearing without any charm at all. Winsome is narrower: fresh, artless charm, usually young and a little shy. Endearing names what the feeling does to us; winsome describes the charmer.
charm's opposite — it rubs everyone wrong
quietly driving people a step back

Old English wynn, 'joy,' survives nowhere else in modern English — winsome is its last address. (The look-alike verb win is a different Old English word, winnan, 'to strive.') The suffix -some, though, is alive and well: handsome, tiresome, quarrelsome.
Winsome means charming, pleasing.
What wins the judges is the young fiddler's winsome stage manner: the bashful bow, the grin at her own wrong note, the little wave to row three.
Winsome charm is innocent and unstudied — it invites affection rather than commanding admiration.
A movie star is glamorous; a puppy is winsome.
The word leans toward the young, the shy, and the sweet, and it never describes charm that knows its own power.
Winsome praises charm that doesn't know it's charming — childlike, shy, freckled charm.
Charming is the all-purpose word; endearing stresses the fondness produced; glamorous is charm with stage lighting.
In this unit, winsome describes the person; captivate names what their charm does to the rest of us.

The botanical garden's summer walks were usually led by Dr.
Halloran, a man of encyclopedic knowledge and no detectable warmth.
This June he was out sick, so the job fell to Priya, a nineteen-year-old volunteer who had never led anything in her life.

She turned out to be winsome in a way no training could produce: she blushed when she misremembered a Latin name, laughed at her own wrong turns on the path, and crouched beside the smallest visitors to show them moss under a hand lens.
Attendance, steady for years at a dozen, tripled by the third week.
Regulars admitted they came less for the plants than for the guide, though Priya seemed genuinely unaware of that -- which, everyone agreed, was half of it.
